passage: Note from the hostel warden, Thursday evening. Five second-year students sat in the common room with a single sheet of paper for nearly an hour. Nikita read each item aloud: "Bus both ways, a room for four nights, meals, and tickets for the sights. Prices drift upward, so let's pad the total by a tenth." Pema said padding felt like cheating on the maths, then agreed once Nikita reminded everyone how much the fare rose last year. Pema divided the grand total by five and circled the answer at the bottom. "That is what each of us has to save before March." I stayed out of it. Afterwards I only asked if their families had heard the figure. Two had not, and went to phone home.

qa.q: How many students sat with the sheet, and what did Pema divide the grand total by?
qa.a: Five second-year students sat with the sheet, and Pema divided the grand total by five.

qa.q: Why did Pema feel uneasy about the extra amount at first?
qa.a: Pema felt that padding the total was a kind of cheating on the maths. Nikita's reminder about last year's fare rise changed Pema's mind.

qa.q: What else could the group add to this plan, and why would it help?
qa.a: They could hold a spare day and choose refundable seats, because extra money alone does not cover a delayed bus.

qa.q: How might a member with a small allowance see the circled figure?
qa.a: Someone with little spare money may worry that the number is too high, so the group should ask openly whether everyone can manage it.

grounding: Students list the trip's costs, add a cushion and divide by the number of travellers to find each person's saving target.

subtype: Approach: working backward from dates and exams [Thinking]
passage: In the students' union room the exam timetable and the hostel holiday list lay side by side on the table. Yamini ran a pencil down both. "Exams end on the ninth and the hostel shuts on the sixteenth. Only one stretch works for all of us." Farida groaned that there had to be another option, checked again, and found none. "Then train seats come first," Yamini said, "because everything else hangs on the day we leave. A room is easy to find once we know when we arrive." Farida wrote the dates on the board under the word TRAINS and left STAY blank for the following week. Two other members nodded, relieved that someone had finally chosen an order to work in.

qa.q: On which dates did Yamini say the exams end and the hostel shuts?
qa.a: The exams end on the ninth and the hostel shuts on the sixteenth.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when Yamini said only one stretch worked?
qa.a: Farida felt frustrated and hoped for another option. After checking again Farida accepted that there was none.

qa.q: What could the group add to this plan, and why?
qa.a: They could keep a spare day at the end of the window and prefer refundable seats, since one fixed slot leaves no room if a train is cancelled.

qa.q: How might the two quieter members see Yamini's decision to fix the trains first?
qa.a: They felt relieved, because the group had been going in circles and now knew what to do next.

grounding: A group fits a trip around exam dates and holidays, books the dependent item first and settles the rest afterwards.

subtype: Approach: a shared expense sheet and advance deposit [Action]
passage:
Saturday. Tushar opened a shared sheet with columns for date, item, who paid and amount. Six friends each sent a first deposit into one account, and Harish took charge of checking that all six had arrived.

Tuesday, on the road. Every ticket, tea stop and cab fare went into the sheet within the hour. When the guesthouse was paid from the pooled money, Harish pinned the receipt photo beside that row.

The Monday after. The sheet showed a small balance left over. Nobody asked who owed what. Tushar split the remainder six ways and sent each share back. Harish said quietly that the sheet had settled the argument before it could start. Two friends who had quarrelled over a trip last year just laughed and closed the laptop.

qa.q: How many friends sent a first deposit into the one account?
qa.a: Six friends each sent a first deposit into one account.

qa.q: Why did Harish say quietly that the sheet had settled the argument before it started?
qa.a: Harish felt relieved, because every payment was written down and nobody had to argue about who owed what. 🙂

qa.q: What alternative could work if someone forgets to log a payment on the road?
qa.a: They could pick one person to review the sheet each night, since small gaps are easier to fix on the same day.

qa.q: How might the two friends who quarrelled last year see this trip?
qa.a: They may see it as a calmer trip, because the sheet answered the money questions that caused trouble before.

grounding: A group opens a shared sheet, pays in advance and logs every expense, which avoids later disputes over money.

subtype: Approach: leaving planning to the last moment [Pitfall]
passage: Club mentor's note, written after the third meeting. For six weeks Vinita and the others repeated the same line whenever the coast trip came up: "We'll figure it out later." Nobody looked at fares. Afreen said twice that someone should book, and both times the talk drifted to other things. When the group finally sat down, the trains for the planned dates were full and the guesthouse price had climbed. They could only afford one night instead of three. Two members dropped out. Vinita was quiet for a long while and said, "We had time and we wasted it." I did not lecture. I asked what one booking they could make before the next meeting. Afreen answered, "Tickets, tonight," and opened the booking page.

qa.q: How many nights could the group afford in the end?
qa.a: They could only afford one night instead of three.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when saying they had time and wasted it?
qa.a: Vinita felt regret and disappointment. The remark shows Vinita knew the delay caused the loss.

qa.q: What approach could have worked better, and why?
qa.a: Fixing a booking date at the first meeting would have worked, because early fares were still available and the choice could have been made calmly.

qa.q: How might the two members who dropped out see the plan?
qa.a: They may feel let down, since they waited weeks for a plan and then found the trip cut down before they could decide.

grounding: A group postpones planning until fares rise and trains fill, so the trip shrinks and people are disappointed.

subtype: Approach: pooling ideas then agreeing a shortlist [Thinking]
passage: Lecturer's note from the study-tour committee meeting. I lent the seminar room and watched. Each of the six students wrote two must-see places on the board. Farida counted them and said, "That's twelve stops. In four days we would spend the whole trip on trains." Francis suggested keeping only the places that sat close together and asking who would give up their second choice before their first. People laughed, and then most agreed. They voted, and the compact route kept one top pick for every person, with two long detours dropped. Francis read the final list aloud once more to check that nobody's first choice was missing. Nobody was. I signed the room register and left them to book.

qa.q: How many places did the students put on the board in total?
qa.a: There were twelve stops on the board, two from each of the six students.

qa.q: Why did Farida feel the plan needed to change when counting the stops?
qa.a: Farida worried that twelve stops would eat the whole trip on trains, so a shorter route was needed.

qa.q: What could the group try next if two top picks turn out to be far apart?
qa.a: They could split one day into two short options and let people choose, because each person still sees their top pick.

qa.q: How might a student whose second choice was dropped see the vote?
qa.a: They may feel a small disappointment but accept it, since their first choice was still on the route and the group agreed openly.

grounding: Students gather their must-do places, see that all cannot fit, and vote for a compact route that keeps each person's top pick.

subtype: Approach: groupthink over an unaffordable plan [Pitfall]
passage: Thursday night, hostel. Today the group locked the beach plan and everyone said "sounds great". So did I. The total per head is far above what my monthly allowance can carry, and I kept telling myself I'd manage. I could not bring myself to call it too much when the others looked so pleased. Deposit was due at four and I skipped canteen lunches all week to make it. I told Bhavna I had a headache when they went for dinner, because I could not pay for that as well. Tonight the chat is full of packing lists and I feel outside it, like a guest at my own trip. I should have spoken on Monday. Signed, Harsha.

qa.q: What did Harsha skip all week to make the deposit?
qa.a: Harsha skipped canteen lunches all week to make the deposit.

qa.q: Why did Harsha say "sounds great" along with the others?
qa.a: Harsha felt unable to be the one to say the plan was too costly when everyone looked pleased, so Harsha stayed quiet and felt excluded.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Harsha have used, and why?
qa.a: Harsha could have asked privately for a cheaper option before the group locked the plan, because a quiet word is easier than speaking up in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see the headache excuse?
qa.a: Bhavna may have believed the excuse and not guessed the money problem, which means the group missed the chance to change the plan.

grounding: A member with a tight allowance stays silent about a costly plan, then struggles to pay and feels left out.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for weather and delays [Thinking]
passage: Elizabeth stirred her tea and told Zeenat about her own college trip to the hills. "Before we left, I asked what could go wrong. A landslide could block the road. A bus could run late. So I said, keep one spare day at the end. Book the stays that allow a refund, where we can. And write down three things to do indoors, in case it pours." Somebody laughed at the list. Then a slide really did close the road for a day. "The spare day meant nobody missed an exam. The refund saved us money. And we played cards in a tea shop and enjoyed it." She tapped the table. "The plan was not to stop bad luck. It was to make sure bad luck did not wreck everything."

qa.q: What three things did Elizabeth's group prepare in advance?
qa.a: They kept one spare day, booked refundable stays where possible and wrote down three indoor things to do.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth thinking when she asked what could go wrong?
qa.a: Elizabeth worried that a landslide or a late bus could wreck the trip, so she wanted a plan for those possibilities before leaving.

qa.q: What could the group have done if no refundable stay was available?
qa.a: They could choose the cheapest option with a free change date or keep a small emergency amount, because it still limits the cost of a delay.

qa.q: How might someone with an exam at the end of the trip have seen the spare day?
qa.a: That friend would feel relieved, since the spare day meant the exam was not missed when the road closed.

grounding: An elder recalls preparing for landslides and delays with a spare day, refundable bookings and indoor options, and how it helped.

passage:
Subject: Thanks for the call

Hi Hrithik,

I wanted to write down what we agreed so nothing gets lost. You will take the smaller room option, which is the cheaper one, and the rest of us will take the standard rooms. Cabs, the boat ride and the group dinner get split equally between all five of us. Nobody has to explain or apologise for anything, and I'll share the sheet tonight so you can see every number.

Thank you for saying your budget out loud. I know it wasn't easy, and it made the plan better for all of us. If any figure feels off once you see it, tell me and we will fix it together. 🙂

Ojas

qa.q: Which costs will be split equally between all five of them?
qa.a: Cabs, the boat ride and the group dinner will be split equally between all five of them.

qa.q: What might Ojas be feeling while thanking Hrithik for saying the budget out loud?
qa.a: Ojas feels grateful and understanding, and knows it was not easy for Hrithik to speak about money.

qa.q: What other approach could the group try if the cheaper room turns out to be unpleasant?
qa.a: They could look again together for another mid-priced option, because sharing the choice keeps Hrithik from carrying the problem alone.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the arrangement compared with quietly paying more than possible?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel respected and relaxed, since the cheaper room was agreed openly and nobody was embarrassed.

grounding: A group member writes to confirm an open agreement where the member with a smaller allowance takes a cheaper room and shared costs are split equally.

subtype: Approach: informing parents with itinerary and contacts [Action]
passage: The train left at five the next morning, and it was already ten at night. Dolma typed the plan into a note: dates, the guesthouse address, and the phone number of the owner, which was still missing. Siddharth called the booking site and waited eleven minutes on hold before getting the number. Both of them sent the note to their families, the last message with the owner's number added at the bottom. Siddharth's mother replied with a single line asking them to send a message on arriving. In the hills the signal would be patchy, so they turned on live location for the group before leaving the city. Dolma slept badly but felt calmer, knowing home could reach them.

qa.q: What was still missing from the note when Dolma typed the plan?
qa.a: The phone number of the guesthouse owner was still missing from the note.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel after the families had the details?
qa.a: Dolma felt calmer despite sleeping badly, because home would be able to reach them.

qa.q: What else could the travellers do if there is no signal in the hills?
qa.a: They could agree on fixed times to send a short message whenever there is signal, since a routine keeps families reassured.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's mother see the shared note and location?
qa.a: Siddharth's mother is likely to feel reassured, because she has the address, the phone numbers and a way to check in.

grounding: Travellers share their itinerary, stay address and contact number with their families and keep live location on, despite a late-night rush.

subtype: Approach: replanning when money runs short mid-trip [Revision]
passage:
Friday evening. Vishal and Yamini paid for the first day's boat ride, lunch and an entry fee, and everyone posted photos, feeling pleased.

Saturday morning. Before setting out, Yamini added up the sheet over tea and said, "We have spent almost half of what we planned for the whole trip, and it is only day two." Nobody argued. Vishal suggested crossing off the paid fort tour, and the group agreed. Yamini offered to cook one meal in the guesthouse kitchen.

Monday. They walked to two free viewpoints and cooked dal and rice at the guesthouse. The sheet showed spending back on track. Vishal said it was the cheapest day and possibly the best one.

qa.q: What did Vishal suggest crossing off on Saturday morning?
qa.a: Vishal suggested crossing off the paid fort tour.

qa.q: Why did Yamini feel worried while adding up the sheet over tea?
qa.a: Yamini worried because almost half of the trip's money was gone by day two, so the plan needed to change.

qa.q: What other approach could work if the money runs short again?
qa.a: They could set a daily spending limit each morning, because a small limit shows problems earlier than a total at the end.

qa.q: How might a group member who had wanted the fort tour see the change?
qa.a: That friend may feel disappointed at first, but seeing the group choose free viewpoints instead of ending the trip could make the loss easier to accept.

grounding: On day two a group sees spending is above plan and adjusts by cutting a paid activity, cooking once and using free views.
